name: Daria Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a garage on the bypass that does most of the servicing for a local taxi firm, plus private cars. The taxis are hybrids doing huge miles, so it's brakes, tyres, suspension and oil, over and over. I use AI every day for quotes, for reading fault codes and for teaching myself the jobs I'm still slow at. I like the routine and I like that the taxi drivers rely on us, and I hate being the one who takes twice as long on a strut.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home and money look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my nan, who raised me, and I help her with the shopping and the bills. My pay's low because I'm still junior, and I've got under a month saved. There's this garage, a main dealer that wants qualifications I don't have, and that's about it nearby. On Sundays I buy cheap old cars, fix them up and sell them on, which is where any spare money comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's a useful tool, and anyone who works hard can use it to get ahead. I'd keep posting the cars I've fixed up, with AI-written adverts. I'd say the doom talk was nonsense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine, but money's tight and Nan's getting frail. If she needs more care, it's on me, and that's time and money I don't have. AI doesn't change that either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the garage and do one more car flip a month if I could find the cars. I'd keep using AI for quotes and learning. I'd start putting the flip profit aside for Nan rather than spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about Nan. Fine about the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does a car flip make you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two or three hundred if I'm lucky, sometimes nothing. Last month I bought a hatchback with a dead clutch and made two hundred and forty after parts. AI helped me find the cheapest clutch kit in about five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if your nan needed more care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my hours or ask the garage for earlier finishes. My uncle would chip in a bit, he lives two hours away. We look after our own in my family.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, and hard workers can use it to get ahead.
think: Money's tight and **Nan's getting frail**, which AI doesn't change.
If Nan needs **more care**, it falls on me.
do: Do **one more car flip** a month if I can find cars.
Keep using **AI for quotes** and learning.
Set aside **flip profit** for Nan's care.
S0.quote: Last month I bought a hatchback with a dead clutch and made two hundred and forty after parts.
fieldNote: Daria's main pressure is **caring for her nan**, not technology.
She already runs a **side business** flipping cars with AI help.
Her values centre on **family** looking after its own.

steps.text: Keep servicing the taxi fleet at the bypass garage
Flip one extra used car a month
Set aside car flip profits for Nan's care

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people willing to learn, and that the government shouldn't get in the way. Businesses that adapt will win. I'd say work hard and use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm alright for a while. I already use AI for the thinking side, and the taxis still need brakes and tyres done by hand. The risk is the taxi firm getting software that books its own servicing with whoever's cheapest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the garage if I can handle the taxi firm's account, the bookings and the quotes, using AI. I'd do the high-voltage course, because the hybrids need it. I'd grow the flipping into a proper sideline, maybe two cars a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, with a bit of nerves about the taxi contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government shouldn't get in the way. What about people who can't adapt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families and churches should help first, and people should be pushed to learn. I'd help someone at the garage, gladly. I just don't think handouts fix anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would losing the taxi contract mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing the taxi contract would mean half our work gone overnight, and I'd be the first junior out. So I'd want to be the person the taxi boss talks to.

say: It's a **chance** for people willing to learn, and government shouldn't interfere.
Businesses that **adapt** will win, so work hard and use the tools.
think: I already do the **thinking side** with AI, and taxis need hands-on work.
The taxi firm could use software to **book the cheapest** garage.
do: Ask to run the **taxi firm's account** with AI quotes and bookings.
Take the **high-voltage course** for the hybrids.
Grow car flipping to **two cars a month**.
feel: Mostly **good**, with **nerves** about the taxi contract.
S1.quote: Losing the taxi contract would mean half our work gone overnight, and I'd be the first junior out.
fieldNote: Daria sees **opportunity**, planning to own the key client relationship.
Her traditional views favour **family help** over handouts, but she'd help colleagues.
The **taxi contract** is her single point of failure.

steps.text: Ask to run the taxi firm's bookings and quotes using AI
Flip two used cars a month on Sundays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people should get busy, not wait for the government. Find what still needs doing and do it. That's what I'd tell my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the taxi firm goes driverless and the carmakers service their own robotaxis. That's half our work, maybe more. Then robots do the brakes by 2031, so even private cars don't need me. I'm twenty-seven with my nan to look after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the car flipping as hard as I can now, because people will still buy and sell old cars for a while. I'd try to get a job with whoever services the robotaxis, even as a trainee. I'd cut out anything extra and save every penny for Nan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried sick about Nan, honestly. For me, I'd find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd find something. What if nothing's there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nan's bills don't care what job I do. I'd take any work going, cleaning, delivery, anything. I'm not proud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your family step in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle would help with Nan, and I'd ask him to. That's what family is for. I'd rather that than a care home.

say: It's a **shock**, but people should get busy, not wait for government.
Find what **still needs doing** and do it.
think: The taxi firm goes **driverless**, and carmakers service their own robotaxis.
Robots do brakes by **2031**, and I've got Nan to look after.
do: Push **car flipping** hard while people still trade old cars.
Apply to **robotaxi servicing** firms, even as a trainee.
feel: **Worried sick** about Nan, sure I'd find something for myself.
S2.quote: Nan's bills don't care what job I do. I'd take any work going, cleaning, delivery, anything.
fieldNote: Daria spots a specific threat: **robotaxis** serviced by carmakers in-house.
Her fear centres on **caring for her nan**, not her own pride.
She'd turn to **her uncle** before any state help.

steps.text: Flip as many used cars as possible each month
Apply for trainee jobs servicing robotaxis
Save every spare penny for Nan's care
Ask her uncle to share Nan's care and costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've had a warning, so use it. Learn, start something, don't wait to be rescued. That's my whole view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to build the car business into something real. AI takes over quoting and diagnosis by 2031, but I'm using it already. Then robots in 2034, and by then I want to be the owner, not the junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the high-voltage course and keep the garage job for steady money. I'd grow flipping to a small used car business with a proper yard, maybe rent a lock-up in year two. I'd save hard and keep Nan's money separate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I like a challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying and selling cars exposed too, if AI does the selling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, yeah. AI can write the advert and set the price. But someone still has to look at a rusty sill and decide if a car's worth saving, until 2034 at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop and play it safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nan getting worse. If she needs me at home, the yard waits. Family first.

say: We've had **a warning** about AGI, so let's use the five years well.
Learn, **start something**, and don't wait around to be rescued.
think: Five years is enough to grow the **car business** into something real.
By **2034** I want to be the owner, not the junior.
do: Do the **high-voltage course** and keep the garage job for steady pay.
Rent a **lock-up** in year two for the car business.
Save hard and keep **Nan's money** separate.
S3.quote: Someone still has to look at a rusty sill and decide if a car's worth saving, until 2034 at least.
fieldNote: Five years lets Daria aim at **ownership** through a small used car yard.
She accepts AI will take pricing and adverts, keeping the **hands-on judgement**.
**Nan's health** is the one thing that would stop the plan.

steps.text: Rent a lock-up in year two for a used car business
Save hard and keep Nan's care money separate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. Nobody owes us a living. I'd say get a trade and build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one suits me. Robots in 2039, I'd be thirty-nine and could have a decent little business by then. The worry is Nan, who won't be here forever, and I want to give her some good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the car business slowly, the high-voltage course first, then the lock-up, then a small yard. I'd use AI for every bit of the selling and paperwork. I'd save enough so Nan never has to worry about her bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the business look like in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe me and an apprentice, fixing up older hybrids and selling them to people who can't afford new. Maybe robots doing some of the work by then. I'd own the robots, not work for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently for yourself, not Nan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe find a partner and settle down, once things are steady. I've put that off for Nan and the job. Ten years is enough time to fit it in.

say: Ten years is **plenty** for anyone willing to work.
**Nobody owes us** a living, so get a trade and build something.
think: Robots in **2039** give me time to build a decent business.
The worry is **Nan**, and giving her some good years.
do: Build the **car business** slowly: course, lock-up, then a small yard.
S4.quote: I'd own the robots, not work for them.
fieldNote: A decade lets Daria plan to **own robots** rather than compete with them.
She has put **personal life** on hold for her nan and her work.
Her free-market view shapes a **self-reliant** business plan.

steps.text: Open a small used hybrid car yard over ten years
Use AI for car adverts, pricing and paperwork
Save enough to cover Nan's bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because of Nan, not me. I'd scrape by, but looking after Nan on no money is the scary bit. What would help is small business loans for people like me, and help for families caring for older relatives at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the people caring for someone. Half my friends look after a parent or grandparent. Any change hits carers twice, because there's someone at home depending on our wage.

headlineQuote: Any change hits carers twice, because there's someone at home depending on our wage.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old** junior at a bypass garage that services a local taxi fleet.
She lives with and **cares for her nan**, with under a month of savings.
She uses AI **every day** and flips cheap used cars on Sundays for extra money.
She believes in **self-reliance** and family help over government support.
Her biggest risk is **robotaxis** taking the fleet work, and her biggest worry is Nan.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, leaving her unable to fund **Nan's care**.
whatWouldHelp: Small **business loans** and support for **family carers** at home.
